source_refs.note: Exercise 11.3, Question 7: book page 295. The book prints no answers for Unit 11.

blocks.prompt: 7 (a) A comet orbits the Sun in an elliptical path such that its position (in AU) at time \(t\) (in years) is described by \(x = 2\cos t, y = \sin t\). Write the position vector \(\mathbf{r}(t)\).
blocks.explanation:
The two coordinates are given; a position vector just puts them together.
Find: \(\mathbf{r}(t) = x\,\hat{i} + y\,\hat{j}\).
Plan: write the vector and check that it traces an ellipse.
steps:
Given: \(x = 2\cos t\), \(y = \sin t\).
To find: \(\mathbf{r}(t)\).
Method: \(\mathbf{r}(t) = x(t)\,\hat{i} + y(t)\,\hat{j}\) (component form, 11.1.3).

Position vector
\[\mathbf{r}(t) = 2\cos t\,\hat{i} + \sin t\,\hat{j}\]
Why: each coordinate becomes the component along its axis.

Check: the path is an ellipse
\[\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)^{2} + y^{2} = \cos^{2}t + \sin^{2}t = 1\]
\[\dfrac{x^{2}}{4} + y^{2} = 1\]
Why: this is an ellipse with semi-axes 2 (along \(x\)) and 1 (along \(y\)), as the question says.
blocks.final_answer: \(\mathbf{r}(t) = 2\cos t\,\hat{i} + \sin t\,\hat{j}\) (AU); its path is the ellipse \(\frac{x^{2}}{4} + y^{2} = 1\).

blocks.prompt: 7 (b) A comet orbits the Sun in an elliptical path such that its position (in AU) at time \(t\) (in years) is described by \(x = 2\cos t, y = \sin t\). Find the velocity and speed at \(t = \frac{\pi}{2}\).
blocks.explanation:
Velocity is \(\mathbf{r}'(t)\) and speed is its magnitude.
Find: \(\mathbf{v}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) and \(\left|\mathbf{v}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\right|\).
Plan: differentiate part (a), substitute, take the magnitude.
steps:
Given: \(\mathbf{r}(t) = 2\cos t\,\hat{i} + \sin t\,\hat{j}\).
To find: velocity and speed at \(t = \frac{\pi}{2}\).
Method: \(\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{r}'\), speed \(= |\mathbf{v}|\).

Velocity
\[\mathbf{v}(t) = -2\sin t\,\hat{i} + \cos t\,\hat{j}\]
\[\mathbf{v}\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = -2\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2}\,\hat{i} + \cos\tfrac{\pi}{2}\,\hat{j}\]
\[= -2\,\hat{i} + 0\,\hat{j}\]
Why: \(\frac{d}{dt}(2\cos t) = -2\sin t\), \(\frac{d}{dt}\sin t = \cos t\); \(\sin\frac{\pi}{2} = 1\), \(\cos\frac{\pi}{2} = 0\).

Speed
\[\left|\mathbf{v}\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\right| = \sqrt{(-2)^{2} + 0^{2}} = 2\]
Why: magnitude of the velocity.

Meaning
At \(t = \frac{\pi}{2}\) the comet is at \(\mathbf{r} = 0\,\hat{i} + \hat{j}\), the point \((0, 1)\) at the top of the ellipse, moving in the negative \(x\)-direction at 2 AU per year. Check: the velocity \(-2\,\hat{i}\) is horizontal, which is the tangent direction at the top of the ellipse.

blocks.prompt: 7 (c) A comet orbits the Sun in an elliptical path such that its position (in AU) at time \(t\) (in years) is described by \(x = 2\cos t, y = \sin t\). Show that the acceleration vector always points toward the origin.
blocks.explanation:
A 'show that' question: we must prove it for every \(t\), not just one instant.
Find \(\mathbf{a}(t)\) and compare it with \(\mathbf{r}(t)\).
Plan: if \(\mathbf{a}(t)\) is a negative multiple of \(\mathbf{r}(t)\), it points from the comet back to the origin.
steps:
Given: \(\mathbf{v}(t) = -2\sin t\,\hat{i} + \cos t\,\hat{j}\) from part (b).
To prove: \(\mathbf{a}(t)\) points towards the origin for every \(t\).
Method: differentiate \(\mathbf{v}(t)\) and write the result in terms of \(\mathbf{r}(t)\).

Acceleration
\[\mathbf{a}(t) = \mathbf{v}'(t) = -2\cos t\,\hat{i} - \sin t\,\hat{j}\]
\[= -\left(2\cos t\,\hat{i} + \sin t\,\hat{j}\right)\]
\[= -\mathbf{r}(t)\]
Why: \(\frac{d}{dt}(-2\sin t) = -2\cos t\), \(\frac{d}{dt}\cos t = -\sin t\); then take out the common factor \(-1\).

Direction
\(\mathbf{r}(t)\) points from the origin \(O\) to the comet, so \(-\mathbf{r}(t)\) points from the comet back to \(O\). Since \(\mathbf{a}(t) = (-1)\mathbf{r}(t)\) for every \(t\), the acceleration always points towards the origin.
Why: multiplying a vector by a negative number reverses its direction.

Check
At \(t = \frac{\pi}{2}\): \(\mathbf{r} = \hat{j}\) and \(\mathbf{a} = -\hat{j}\), pointing straight down from \((0, 1)\) to \(O\). (Note, ours: in this simplified model the centre of attraction is the centre \(O\) of the ellipse; for a real comet the Sun is at a focus, but the method is the same.)
blocks.final_answer: Hence proved: \(\mathbf{a}(t) = -\mathbf{r}(t)\) for every \(t\), which is opposite to the position vector, so the acceleration always points towards the origin.

blocks.text: The textbook prints no answers for Exercise 11.3 (it prints no answers for any exercise of Unit 11). Every answer on this page is ours: worked out step by step, checked independently with a computer algebra system (sympy) and compared with a solution book. Angles such as \(t = \frac{\pi}{2}\) are in radians.
